title: Smooth Muscle and the Myogenic Response

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In smooth muscle, what sets the fraction p of myosin light chains that carry a phosphate at any moment?
cards.back: The balance of two enzymes: myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) adds the phosphate and myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes it, so p = k_MLCK / (k_MLCK + k_MLCP).
cards.quote: The fraction carrying a phosphate, p, settles at a balance point where the two rates are equal

cards.front: In the smooth muscle balance-point rule, calcium sets the kinase; other signals, {{c1::Rho kinase}} above all, set the phosphatase.
cards.quote: Calcium sets the kinase; other signals, Rho kinase above all, set the phosphatase.

cards.front: In smooth muscle, what does calcium bind to start contraction, and which enzyme does that complex activate?
cards.back: Calmodulin. Calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the 20-kDa regulatory light chain, LC20, so the motor can cycle on actin.
cards.quote: calcium binds calmodulin, calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK), and MLCK puts a phosphate on the 20-kDa regulatory light chain, LC20

cards.front: Why does the calcium switch of smooth muscle sit on myosin rather than on the thin filament?
cards.back: Smooth muscle has no troponin, so calcium cannot act on the thin filament as in skeletal and cardiac muscle; instead calcium-calmodulin turns on MLCK, which switches on the myosin motor.
cards.quote: Smooth muscle has no troponin, so calcium cannot act on the thin filament as it does in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

cards.front: In smooth muscle, depolarization opens L-type calcium channels (CaV1.2) and calcium flows in down its electrochemical gradient: {{c1::electromechanical}} coupling.
cards.quote: Depolarization opens L-type channels (CaV1.2) and calcium flows in down its electrochemical gradient: electromechanical coupling.

cards.front: How can a Gq-coupled agonist contract smooth muscle with little change in membrane potential, and what is this route called?
cards.back: The receptor makes IP3, which opens release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so stored calcium is released without depolarization: pharmacomechanical coupling.
cards.quote: an agonist on a Gq-coupled receptor makes IP3, which opens release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cards.front: Compare where the activating calcium comes from in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.
cards.back: Skeletal: the store only. Cardiac: calcium entering during the action potential triggers a larger release from the store. Smooth: both L-type entry and sarcoplasmic reticulum release.
cards.quote: Both: entry through L-type channels and release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cards.front: Calcium is removed from the solution outside a skeletal muscle fibre and outside a smooth muscle strip. Which loses more of its ability to contract when depolarized, and why?
cards.back: The smooth muscle. Its calcium comes partly from entry through L-type channels, while skeletal muscle releases calcium from the store through a mechanical link and needs no calcium from outside.
cards.quote: The store only: a voltage sensor in the T tubule is linked mechanically to the release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so no calcium from outside is needed

cards.front: Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres. Where are its thin filaments anchored?
cards.back: In dense bodies, protein clusters in the cytoplasm, and in dense plaques on the inside of the membrane.
cards.quote: Its thin filaments are anchored instead in dense bodies, protein clusters in the cytoplasm, and in dense plaques on the inside of the membrane.

cards.front: Why can a smooth muscle cell develop force over a much wider range of lengths than skeletal muscle, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Its filaments are not stacked in sarcomeres, so there is no fixed overlap register setting a narrow length-tension curve. That suits an organ that fills.
cards.quote: Because the filaments are not stacked in sarcomeres, the cell can develop force over a much wider range of lengths than a sarcomere can

cards.front: Compared with skeletal muscle, how does smooth muscle shorten and hold force, and why?
cards.back: It generally shortens slowly because its cross-bridges cycle more slowly; above all in tonic smooth muscle, it holds force cheaply through the latch state.
cards.quote: Smooth muscle's cross-bridges also cycle more slowly, so it generally shortens slowly and, above all in tonic smooth muscle, holds force cheaply

cards.front: Illustrative rates in a smooth muscle cell: k_MLCK = 1 and k_MLCP = 4 per second. (a) What fraction p of light chains is phosphorylated? (b) A Rho kinase signal cuts k_MLCP to 1 per second with calcium unchanged. What is the new p?
cards.back: (a) p = 1 / (1 + 4) = 0.2. (b) p = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.5. Phosphorylation rises 2.5-fold with no change in calcium: calcium sensitization.
cards.why: At the balance point k_MLCK × (1 − p) = k_MLCP × p, which rearranges to p = k_MLCK / (k_MLCK + k_MLCP).
cards.quote: Step 2, at the balance point the two rates are equal: k_MLCK × (1 − p) = k_MLCP × p.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: While MLCK is active, why does light-chain phosphorylation in smooth muscle settle at a steady level rather than climbing to 100 percent?
cards.back: MLCP never stops removing phosphate. Like a sink with the tap running and the drain open, p settles where phosphates go on exactly as fast as they come off.
cards.quote: A second enzyme, myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), takes the phosphate back off LC20, and it never stops working
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: In smooth muscle, kinase and phosphatase start equally active (p = 0.5). One signal halves the phosphatase and leaves calcium alone. By what factor would calcium have to raise the kinase to reach the same p?
cards.back: Double it. Halving the phosphatase gives p = 1 / (1 + 0.5) = 0.67; doubling the kinase gives 2 / (2 + 1) = 0.67. A signal that never touches calcium can still raise force.
cards.quote: Halving the drain does what doubling the tap does.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: In smooth muscle, calcium {{c1::sensitization}} is any change that buys more force, or more phosphorylation, at an unchanged calcium concentration.
cards.back: Desensitization buys less.
cards.quote: Calcium sensitization is any change that buys more force, or more phosphorylation, at an unchanged calcium concentration; desensitization buys less.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: On a graph of smooth muscle force against calcium, what does calcium sensitization do to the curve?
cards.back: It mainly slides the curve to the left, so less calcium gives the same force.
cards.quote: On a graph of force against calcium, sensitization mainly slides the curve to the left, so less calcium gives the same force.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: How does RhoA raise calcium sensitivity in smooth muscle?
cards.back: RhoA activates Rho kinase (ROCK), which phosphorylates MYPT1, the targeting subunit of the phosphatase, and inhibits MLCP. k_MLCP falls while k_MLCK stays put, so p and force rise.
cards.quote: RhoA activates Rho kinase (ROCK), which phosphorylates MYPT1, the targeting subunit of the phosphatase, and inhibits MLCP.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: An arterial strip is permeabilized so the bath sets intracellular calcium, held at a moderate level. A drug that activates RhoA is added. Predict LC20 phosphorylation and force, and say how you know calcium did not cause the change.
cards.back: Both rise. Rho kinase inhibits the phosphatase, so p rises at the same kinase activity. Calcium cannot have risen because the bath clamps it. This is the experiment that defines sensitization.
cards.quote: Permeabilize a strip of artery so that the bath, not the cell, sets the calcium inside, and hold it at a moderate level.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: In permeabilized rabbit portal vein, the kinase is stopped so only the phosphatase acts. GTP-gamma-S, which keeps G proteins active, slows dephosphorylation and relaxation to about half the control rates. What does this show?
cards.back: A G protein can raise force by slowing dephosphorylation (the drain) even with the kinase stopped. This was early evidence for calcium sensitization.
cards.quote: GTP-gamma-S, which keeps G proteins active, slowed dephosphorylation and relaxation to about half the control rates
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: In smooth muscle, protein kinase C phosphorylates {{c1::CPI-17}}, a protein that then inhibits myosin light-chain phosphatase.
cards.back: A second brake on the phosphatase, besides Rho kinase.
cards.quote: Protein kinase C gives a second brake on the phosphatase: it phosphorylates CPI-17, a protein that inhibits MLCP once it is itself phosphorylated.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: By what pathway does endothelial nitric oxide relax smooth muscle, and which two sides of the kinase-phosphatase balance does it move?
cards.back: NO activates soluble guanylate cyclase; cGMP activates protein kinase G. That lowers calcium (tap down, less kinase) and raises phosphatase activity (drain open).
cards.quote: In muscle that lowers calcium, which turns the tap down, and raises phosphatase activity, which opens the drain.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: In permeabilized rabbit artery with calcium clamped, the cGMP analog 8-bromo-cGMP still relaxes the muscle. What does this rule out, and what mechanism does it point to?
cards.back: It rules out a fall in calcium as the whole explanation, since calcium could not fall. It points to cGMP raising phosphatase activity (read by the authors as indirect activation): desensitization.
cards.quote: In permeabilized rabbit artery with calcium clamped, the cGMP analog 8-bromo-cGMP still relaxed the muscle, which the authors read as indirect activation of the phosphatase.
cards.section: The balance point: kinase against phosphatase

cards.front: What is the latch state of smooth muscle?
cards.back: Force held near its peak during sustained stimulation after LC20 phosphorylation has fallen back toward low values.
cards.quote: Something holds the load after the phosphates come off, and that state is called latch.

cards.front: In the Hai-Murphy model, how does a smooth muscle myosin head keep holding force after its phosphate is removed?
cards.back: A head that loses its phosphate while attached does not release at once. It becomes a latch bridge whose slow detachment keeps it bearing load while cycling rate and ATP cost fall.
cards.why: The slow release is an assumption of a model fitted to phosphorylation and stress data, not an imaged structure.
cards.quote: It becomes a latch bridge, whose slow detachment is the rate-limiting step, so attached heads keep bearing load while the cycling rate, and ATP cost, fall.

cards.front: Is the latch state of smooth muscle a state without ATP use, like rigor? Explain.
cards.back: No. Phosphorylated cross-bridges keep cycling, latch bridges let go slowly and calcium pumps keep working: latch is economy, not shutdown. Rigor is the stiff state of a muscle whose ATP has run out.
cards.quote: Latch is not a state without ATP: phosphorylated cross-bridges keep cycling, latch bridges let go slowly, and calcium pumps keep working, so latch is economy, not shutdown.

cards.front: A few purified smooth muscle myosins in a laser trap reach a force plateau; then phosphatase is injected. Tonic myosin (pig stomach) holds force a median 32 s, phasic (chicken gizzard) 21 s; a parallel assay puts dephosphorylation midpoint near 27 s. What does this support, and why is only the tonic result convincing?
cards.back: It supports latch: force kept as phosphates come off. Only the tonic hold outlasted the dephosphorylation clock. Limits: timing measured indirectly, and purified non-human proteins, not an intact vessel.
cards.quote: only the tonic hold outlasted that clock, so it is the more convincing

cards.front: A tonic smooth muscle has built force. Phosphatase activity is then doubled while calcium stays constant. Using the balance-point rule and the Hai-Murphy model, predict LC20 phosphorylation and force over the next seconds.
cards.back: Phosphorylation falls to a new, lower balance point. Force falls less and more slowly, because heads dephosphorylated while attached become latch bridges that detach slowly.
cards.why: The balance-point rule sets phosphorylation, not force directly; once force is built, latch lets it outlast the phosphate.
cards.quote: The rule sets phosphorylation, not force directly: once force is built, latch lets it outlast the phosphate.

cards.front: What is the myogenic response of small arteries?
cards.back: The muscular coat contracts when stretched by raised pressure and relaxes when tension falls, independently of the central nervous system.
cards.quote: the muscular coat of an artery contracts when stretched and relaxes when tension falls, independently of the central nervous system

cards.front: Why does an isolated artery on a pressure myograph test the myogenic response more cleanly than recordings of limb volume?
cards.back: Limb volume sums arteries, veins and tissue, so it cannot say which vessels responded. A cannulated, pressurized artery with no nerves and no flow still narrows, so the response lies in the vessel wall.
cards.quote: tied between two glass cannulas and pressurized, with no nerves and no flow, they still narrow

cards.front: Mouse mesenteric arteries lacking G12 and G13 in smooth muscle are pressurized from 20 to 140 mmHg, and calcium rises with pressure as normal. Predict myogenic tone and active RhoA, and state the conclusion.
cards.back: Tone is nearly lost and active RhoA is strongly reduced. Calcium alone is not enough: the tap opened but the drain was never narrowed. In these mouse mesenteric arteries tone needed a calcium rise plus Rho-dependent sensitization.
cards.quote: Two requirements, then, in this bed: a calcium rise and Rho-dependent sensitization.

cards.front: On a pressure myograph at one pressure, a small artery measures 200 micrometres in calcium-containing solution and 250 micrometres in calcium-free solution. Tone = 100 × (passive − active) / passive. What is the myogenic tone?
cards.back: Passive (calcium-free) = 250, active = 200. Tone = 100 × (250 − 200) / 250 = 20 percent.
cards.quote: reading active diameter in calcium-containing and passive diameter in calcium-free solution
cards.section: The mouse study and a conflicting result

cards.front: In Poiseuille's law for an idealized vessel, resistance varies as 1 / r to the {{c1::fourth}} power.
cards.back: So a small narrowing gives a large change in resistance.
cards.quote: The fourth power turns a small narrowing into a large change in resistance.

cards.front: An idealized arteriole (rigid tube, steady laminar Newtonian flow) has a 60 mmHg pressure difference and a radius of 100 µm. The difference rises to 90 mmHg. To what radius must the muscle narrow it to hold flow constant, and by what factor does resistance rise?
cards.back: (r2 / r1)⁴ = 60 / 90 = 0.667, so r2 = 100 × 0.667^(1/4) = 90.4 µm, about 10 percent narrower. Resistance rises 1.5-fold, matching the pressure rise.
cards.quote: For flow to stay constant, (r2 / r1)⁴ = 60 / 80 = 0.75, so r2 = 100 × 0.75^(1/4) = 93.1 µm.

cards.front: An idealized arteriole starts at a 60 mmHg pressure difference and radius 100 µm. The difference rises to 75 mmHg and the muscle overshoots, narrowing the radius to 90 µm. What is the new flow relative to baseline?
cards.back: Q2 / Q1 = (75 / 60) × (90 / 100)⁴ = 1.25 × 0.6561 = 0.82, about 18 percent below baseline.
cards.quote: Overshoot and flow falls: at r2 = 90 µm with the gradient at 80 mmHg, Q2 / Q1 = 1.333 × 0.6561 = 0.875, 12.5 percent below baseline.

cards.front: Is steady blood flow the signal that the myogenic mechanism of a small artery senses?
cards.back: No. The muscle reads stretch of its wall; steady flow is a result. A pressure myograph has no flow, yet the artery still narrows.
cards.quote: Steady flow is a result of answering stretch, not the signal the muscle reads: a pressure myograph has no flow at all.

cards.front: Holding flow steady across a range of pressures is called {{c1::autoregulation}}, produced by several mechanisms together.
cards.quote: Holding flow steady across a range of pressures is autoregulation, produced by several mechanisms together

cards.front: Pressure in a small artery rises while endothelial nitric oxide is lost and sympathetic alpha-1 input increases. Using the kinase-phosphatase balance, predict the diameter and segment resistance.
cards.back: Narrower diameter and much higher resistance. Pressure and alpha-1 input each raise calcium and sensitization, and the loss of nitric oxide removes the input that lowers both; resistance rises as 1 / r⁴.
cards.why: Net diameter reflects the combined effect of the three inputs on the same balance.
cards.quote: pressure raises calcium and sensitization, endothelial nitric oxide lowers both, sympathetic alpha-1 input raises both

cards.front: In essential hypertension, small arteries have a narrower lumen at the same transmural pressure (inward remodelling in people; tone is more established in hypertensive rodents). Predict segment resistance and the effect on mean arterial pressure at a given cardiac output.
cards.back: Resistance rises steeply, by the fourth-power law, and higher resistance at a given cardiac output holds mean arterial pressure up: lumen down, resistance up.
cards.quote: Practise the directions: tone up, lumen down, resistance up.

cards.front: After blood loss, pressure in a small artery falls. Predict the local myogenic response, then how the baroreflex changes the final diameter.
cards.back: Wall tension falls, so the muscle tends to relax and segment resistance falls. The baroreflex raises sympathetic outflow, and alpha-1 input pulls the diameter back down. Net diameter is their combined effect.
cards.quote: after blood loss, pressure in a small artery falls, wall tension falls, the muscle tends to relax and lower segment resistance

cards.front: A Rho kinase inhibitor is given to control mouse mesenteric arteries that show myogenic tone. Predict calcium, light-chain phosphorylation, lumen and segment resistance as pressure rises.
cards.back: Calcium still rises with pressure, but with Rho kinase blocked the phosphatase is no longer inhibited, so phosphorylation and tone fall. The lumen widens and, by the fourth-power law (1 / r⁴), resistance falls.
cards.why: In mouse mesenteric arteries, calcium alone was not enough for tone, and a Rho kinase inhibitor blocked the myogenic response.
cards.quote: In control arteries a Rho kinase inhibitor blocked the response.

cards.front: Contrast how a filling hollow organ and a small resistance artery respond to stretch.
cards.back: Visceral smooth muscle shows stress relaxation: tension falls back after the stretch, so pressure rises little during filling. A small resistance artery contracts when transmural pressure rises.
cards.quote: A small resistance artery does the opposite when transmural pressure rises: it contracts.

cards.front: In {{c1::single-unit}} (visceral) smooth muscle, gap junctions couple neighbouring cells electrically, so excitation spreads and the cells contract as one mass.
cards.back: Examples: gut and uterus.
cards.quote: In single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle, gap junctions couple neighbouring cells electrically, so excitation spreads and the cells contract as one mass

cards.front: What defines multi-unit smooth muscle? Give two examples.
cards.back: Cells have little electrical coupling and each is driven by its own nerve terminals, allowing finely graded control. Examples: the iris and the piloerector muscles.
cards.quote: In multi-unit smooth muscle, cells have little electrical coupling and each is driven by its own nerve terminals, allowing finely graded control

cards.front: A drug blocks gap junctions. Predict its effect on coordinated contraction of gut smooth muscle and of iris smooth muscle.
cards.back: Gut: excitation no longer spreads between cells, so they stop contracting as one mass. Iris: little change, since each multi-unit cell is driven by its own nerve terminals.
cards.quote: gap junctions couple neighbouring cells electrically, so excitation spreads and the cells contract as one mass; the gut and uterus are the usual examples

cards.front: Norepinephrine is applied to isolated rat mesenteric resistance vessels and to isolated human detrusor strips. Predict each response and the receptor mainly responsible.
cards.back: The vessels contract, through alpha-1 adrenoceptors. The detrusor relaxes, mainly through beta-3 adrenoceptors as the authors suggested. Receptors, not sympathetic input in general, set the direction.
cards.quote: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 adrenoceptors contracted isolated rat aorta and mesenteric resistance vessels

cards.front: Design experiments on endothelium-denuded rabbit arteries to ask whether a nitric oxide donor relaxes smooth muscle by lowering calcium, lowering calcium sensitivity, or both.
cards.back: Intact strips: contract with an alpha-1 agonist, add the donor, record force and Fura-2 together; relaxation beyond what the calcium-force curve predicts means lost sensitivity. Permeabilized strips with calcium clamped: relaxation by donor or cGMP at fixed calcium shows desensitization is part of the mechanism.
cards.quote: Then clamp calcium: in alpha-toxin-permeabilized strips the bath sets calcium

cards.front: Testing a nitric oxide donor on denuded arterial strips: how is denudation confirmed, and which controls are needed?
cards.back: Acetylcholine no longer relaxes the strips. Controls: time-matched strips with no donor, a guanylate cyclase inhibitor to confirm the cGMP route, and the same starting force each time.
cards.quote: Controls: time-matched strips with no donor, a guanylate cyclase inhibitor to confirm the cGMP route, the same starting force each time.

cards.front: What does the kinase-phosphatase balance-point rule for smooth muscle leave out?
cards.back: Thin-filament proteins such as caldesmon and calponin, kinases that phosphorylate LC20 without calcium, and enzyme saturation (it treats each rate as proportional to its substrate).
cards.quote: It leaves out thin-filament proteins such as caldesmon and calponin, and kinases that phosphorylate LC20 without calcium.
cards.section: What the balance-point rule leaves out
